newsitem.title: BULGARIA: PYRAMID LURES BULGARIANS WITH $20,000 DEPOSITS.
newsitem.headline: PYRAMID LURES BULGARIANS WITH $20,000 DEPOSITS.

text.p: Bulgarian-Russian joint stock company Shahatana, based in Bulgaria's Black Sea port of Varna, claims to offer an investment haven from the country's shaky banking system for deposits ranging from $1,000 to $20,000.

Through advertisements headlined "Medicine against inflation" in the Varna press and on radio stations, Shahatana has collected $20,000 deposits from around 50 Bulgarians, most of whom were businessmen, a company official said.
"Our contracts envisage use of our Varna medical centre free of charge," Shahatana president Anatoliy Chakurov told Reuters by telephone from Varna.
"We are building a similar rehabilitation centre near the Mediterranean in Spain and our depositors will be entitled to holidays there," said Chakurov.
Chakurov said that depositors could draw their money plus maturity payments every six or 12 months.
"Our investment scheme is much safer than most local banks. We offer steady interest and bonuses," said Chakurov.
The depositors are promised a 25 percent annual interest on their dollar savings, while the average interest on dollar deposits in Bulgarian commercial banks is between four and nine percent.
Depositors in many Bulgarian banks have problems drawing their deposits due to blocked settlement.

Deposits in 14 banks, almost one quarter of country's total, have been blocked after the banks were placed under special supervision with the aim of evaluating their financial state and deciding for which of them to seek insolvency procedures through the courts.
Struggling with economic uncertainty, Bulgarians have withdrawn the equivalent of around $500 million from local banks in the past several months.
Under amendments to a Bulgarian deposit guarantee law, personal and company deposits are compensated by the state after a court declares a bank insolvent, which may take between six and 18 months.
Pyramid investment schemes have proved popular in several other ex-communist countries, including Russia and Romania.

Some 30,000 Bulgarians took a bitter lesson in investment last year when $25 million sank into the several get-rich-quick schemes, which involved using income from new investors to buy back shares from old investors at ever-rising prices.
Some of the founders of the pyramids, who fled with the money, are now under arrest while others are being investigated by Bulgarian authorities with the cooperation of Interpol.
Shahatana launched a similar scheme two years ago and paid out its depositors.
"There is nothing illegal in what we are doing and we have a steady flow of depositors," said Chakurov.

Shahatana is a classic example of a foreign exchange pyramid but no claims have been filed against the company by its clients so far and no steps could be taken against it, said an official of the regional prosecutor's office, who declined to be named.

Varna, a busy port near major Black Sea Bulgarian resorts, has traditionally been considered to be more affluent than the rest of the country, where the average state wage is around 10,000 levs a month.
